NCAA Performance Technologies
Recommendations
Comprehensive Action Plan for Baylor Athletics
Prepared by Coach Rash
Baylor University Department of Athletics
March 2026
WORKING DOCUMENT
For internal use. Subject to revision based on stakeholder input.
Table of Contents
Introduction
In March 2026, the NCAA Sport Science Institute published Performance Technologies Recommendations: Responsible Use in Collegiate Athletics, a consensus document developed from the May 2025 NCAA Summit on Performance Technologies. The document provides member schools with a framework for responsibly using performance technologies, organized around five core recommendations: Policy, Education, Data Management, Technology Selection, and Continuous Improvement.
This action plan translates those recommendations into a detailed, Baylor-specific implementation roadmap. Each section includes the NCAA language, what it means for our department, specific action items with assigned deliverables, and draft templates or sample language that the working group can adapt as we move forward.
Baylor Athletics does not currently have formal performance technology policies in place. This plan is designed to build the foundation from scratch, leveraging existing structures (annual compliance sessions, SAAC, campus IT, and legal resources) wherever possible.
How to Use This Document
Each recommendation section follows a consistent structure:
Blue callout box: The NCAA recommendation language, quoted directly.
Gold callout box: The specific NCAA strategy statement being addressed.
"What This Means for Baylor": Plain-language interpretation of how this applies to us.
Key Actions: Checkbox items for the working group to track.
Deliverable: The specific output expected from each action area.
Draft Templates: Sample language, forms, or frameworks ready for adaptation.
Recommendation 1: Policy
What the NCAA Says: It is recommended that schools establish a written plan that addresses the responsible use of performance technologies. Having a written plan can help establish common standards and procedures, increase transparency ,  and address school-specific needs and resources.
What This Means for Baylor
We need a formal, written policy document that serves as the governing framework for how Baylor Athletics uses performance technologies. This is not a one-time exercise. The NCAA expects it to be developed by a cross-functional team, reviewed regularly, and updated as technologies and needs evolve. Every other recommendation in this document (education, data management, purchasing, and feedback) ties back to this written plan.
Strategy 1.1: Assemble a Multidisciplinary Working Group
NCAA Strategy:  Engage a multidisciplinary team in developing, routinely reviewing ,  and revising a written plan, leveraging existing campus resources and systems. Key roles on that team may include, but are not limited to, student-athletes, sports medicine staff, coaches, athletics administration, legal affairs ,  and information technology.
Key Actions:
Identify a chair/lead for the working group. This person should have the organizational authority to coordinate across departments and the bandwidth to drive the process forward. Recommended candidates: Associate AD for Student-Athlete Services, Director of Sports Medicine, or a senior administrator with cross-departmental oversight.
Recruit representatives from each required area. The NCAA specifically names the following roles. Each representative should have decision-making authority or direct access to decision-makers in their area:
Student-Athletes: Minimum two representatives, ideally from different sports and genders. SAAC members or sport captains are strong candidates. Their voice is not advisory; it is essential.
Sports Medicine/Athletic Training: Head athletic trainer or designee. This person will be critical for data management (Rec 3) and ensuring the independent medical authority is protected.
Strength and Conditioning: Director of S&C or senior staff member. S&C is typically the primary operator of wearable technologies and force plates.
Coaching: Minimum two sport representatives from different sports. Coaches are end-users of performance data and need a seat at the table.
Athletics Administration: Associate AD or senior administrator who can approve policy and allocate resources.
Legal Affairs/Compliance: University legal counsel or athletics compliance officer. Essential for data privacy, consent, and regulatory considerations.
Information Technology: Campus IT or athletics IT representative. Responsible for data security, storage, vendor integration, and breach response.
Define the group charter. The working group should have a clear written charter that includes:
Mission: Develop, maintain, and oversee Baylor Athletics' written plan for the responsible use of performance technologies.
Scope: All performance technologies used across Baylor Athletics, including devices, software, apps, and surveys that collect biometric or performance data.
Responsibilities: Draft and maintain the written plan, review and approve new technology purchases, oversee education programs, collect and act on feedback, and ensure compliance with applicable laws.
Meeting cadence: Monthly during initial development (March through June 2026), then quarterly once the plan is established.
Decision-making: Consensus-based where possible; chair breaks ties. Legal has veto authority on compliance matters.
Set the initial meeting schedule. Book monthly meetings through June 2026. The first meeting should focus on reviewing this document and the NCAA source material, and on assigning ownership of plan sections.
Deliverable:
Working Group Charter Document (1-2 pages) documenting mission, membership, roles, meeting cadence, and decision-making process.
Draft Template: Working Group Charter
Section | Content
Purpose | Establish and maintain Baylor Athletics' written plan for the responsible use of performance technologies in alignment with NCAA Sport Science Institute recommendations.
Membership | Chair: [TBD] Student-Athletes: [Names, Sports] Sports Medicine: [Name, Title] S&C: [Name, Title] Coaching: [Name, Sport] and [Name, Sport] Administration: [Name, Title] Legal/Compliance: [Name, Title] IT: [Name, Title]
Meeting Cadence | Monthly (March-June 2026), Quarterly (July 2026 onward)
Responsibilities | 1. Develop written plan 2. Review/approve new technology purchases 3. Oversee education programs 4. Collect and act on feedback 5. Ensure legal/regulatory compliance
Decision Process | Consensus-based; Chair breaks ties. Legal holds veto on compliance matters.
Reporting | Chair reports to [AD/Senior Administrator] after each meeting.
Review | Charter reviewed annually at the first meeting of each academic year.
Strategy 1.2: Draft the Written Plan
NCAA Strategy:  Address school-specific considerations, including how relevant groups will be educated, how data will be managed, how decisions will be made about selecting and implementing new technologies and how continuous improvement will be approached.
The written plan is the central deliverable. It should be a single, comprehensive document (or a policy manual with clearly organized sections) that anyone in the department can reference. Below is the recommended structure and the content each section should address.
Key Actions:
Create a policy document organized around the following sections:
Plan Section | Content to Address | Owner
1. Purpose & Scope | Why the plan exists, what it covers, which technologies and personnel fall under it | Chair
2. Definitions | Performance technology, biometric data, performance data, informed consent, data steward, etc. | Chair + Legal
3. Roles & Responsibilities | Who does what : Working Group, coaches, S&C, sports medicine, IT, student-athletes, administration | Chair
4. Student-Athlete Rights | Informed consent process, right to decline, data access rights, grievance process | Legal
5. Data Governance | Data ownership, storage, access controls, retention, transfer protocol, breach response (see Rec 3) | IT + Legal
6. Technology Evaluation | Criteria and process for vetting new technologies before purchase (see Rec 4) | S&C + Sports Med
7. Education Requirements | Who gets trained, how often, on what topics, and how completion is tracked (see Rec 2) | Chair
8. Continuous Improvement | Feedback mechanisms, annual review process, plan revision protocol (see Rec 5) | Chair
9. Compliance | Applicable laws (FERPA, state privacy, biometric), NCAA guidance references, institutional policies | Legal + Compliance
10. Appendices | Consent form template, tech evaluation checklist, education curriculum outlines, feedback survey | Various
Route the draft through legal affairs and compliance for review. Legal should review for: applicable privacy laws (FERPA, Texas data privacy, any biometric privacy considerations), adequacy of informed consent language, data breach notification obligations, and alignment with university-wide policies.
Establish version control. Use a naming convention (e.g., BaylorAthletics_PerfTech_Policy_v1.0_2026-06) and maintain a revision log on the first page of the document. Store the master copy in a central location accessible to all working group members.
Set an annual review date. The plan should be reviewed at least annually. Recommend tying the review to the start of each academic year (August/September) so updates can be communicated during preseason meetings.
Deliverable:
Baylor Athletics Performance Technology Policy (estimated 15-25 pages with appendices). Target completion: June 2026.
Milestone | Description | Target Date
Working Group Formed | Chair identified, members recruited, charter signed | March 2026
First Meeting | Review  the  NCAA document, assign plan sections to owners | Early April 2026
Section Drafts Due | Each owner submits their section draft to the chair | Late April 2026
Full Draft Assembled | Chair compiles all sections into  a  unified document | Early May 2026
Legal/Compliance Review | Legal reviews full draft, provides redlines | Mid-May 2026
Working Group Final Review | Group reviews legal feedback, makes final edits | Late May 2026
Plan Approved | Chair and AD sign off; plan distributed to department | June 2026
First Annual Review | Working group reviews and updates the plan | August/September 2026
Recommendation 2: Education
What the NCAA Says: It is recommended that schools routinely provide education about the responsible use of performance technologies to those involved with their use. Education is foundational for informed consent, and it aids in ensuring schools use performance technologies in a way that maximizes benefits and minimizes harm to student-athletes.
What This Means for Baylor
Everyone who touches performance technology needs training, and that training needs to happen at least once a year. The good news: Baylor already has annual compliance and onboarding sessions. We can build performance technology modules into those existing structures rather than creating an entirely new training apparatus. The key is tailoring the content to different audiences, because a student-athlete and a compliance officer need very different information.
Strategy 2.1: Provide Annual Education to All Involved
NCAA Strategy:  At least once annually, provide education to those involved in selecting, using or accessing data from performance technologies.
Key Actions:
Map every person/role that interacts with performance technology. Create a comprehensive list of who selects, operates, interprets, accesses, or makes decisions based on performance technology data. This becomes your required-training roster.
Integrate performance technology training into existing annual sessions:
Staff annual compliance meeting: Add a 30-45 minute performance technology module covering policy overview, data handling responsibilities, and any updates from the previous year.
New student-athlete orientation: Add a 20-30 minute segment on performance technology rights, informed consent, what data is collected, and how to raise concerns.
Returning student-athlete preseason meeting: Add a brief (10-15 minute) refresher covering any new technologies introduced, policy changes, or updated consent requirements.
New hire onboarding: Include performance technology policy review for any new coaches, S&C staff, athletic trainers, or administrators.
Create an attendance tracking system. Use sign-in sheets or digital tracking (LMS if available) to document who completed training and when. This is your compliance record if questions arise.
Store all training materials centrally. Maintain a shared folder (e.g., on the athletics shared drive or LMS) with all slide decks, handouts, and reference materials so staff can review them at any time.
Deliverable:
An annual education calendar that maps each audience to their training session, timing, and delivery method.
Draft Template: Annual Education Calendar
Audience | Session | Timing | Duration | Delivery | Tracked?
All Staff | Annual Compliance Meeting | August (preseason) | 30-45 min | In-person | Sign-in sheet
New Student-Athletes | Orientation | August/January | 20-30 min | In-person | Sign-in sheet
Returning SAs | Preseason Meeting | August | 10-15 min | In-person | Sign-in sheet
New Hires | Onboarding | Within 30 days of hire | 30 min | 1-on-1 or small group | HR checklist
Working Group | Annual Review Meeting | September | 60-90 min | In-person | Meeting minutes
Strategy 2.2: Tailor Education by Audience
NCAA Strategy:  Educational needs are likely to vary among different groups and schools should consider tailoring education to meet each group's learning needs. Such groups may include, but are not limited to, student-athletes, coaches, strength and conditioning staff, sports medicine staff and administration.
A one-size-fits-all presentation will not work. Below is a detailed breakdown of what each audience needs to know, along with sample talking points and curriculum outlines.
Key Actions:
Develop a Student-Athlete Education Module covering:
What performance technologies are and why Baylor uses them.
Exactly what data is collected about them (types, frequency, devices).
Who can see their data and who cannot (access controls by role).
How their data is stored, how long it is kept, and what happens when they graduate or transfer.
Their right to informed consent: what they are agreeing to, that participation is voluntary, how to withdraw, and that declining will not affect their standing on the team.
Potential negative effects to watch for (data fixation, anxiety about metrics, body image concerns from body composition tracking) and who to talk to if they experience them.
How to raise concerns or file a complaint about how their data is being used.
Draft Template: Sample Student-Athlete Talking Points
Topic | Key Message
What We Collect | We use [GPS trackers/heart rate monitors/body comp tools/wellness surveys/etc.] to help us keep you healthy and help you perform your best. Here is specifically what each tool measures.
Who Sees It | Your data is shared only with [specific roles]. Coaches can see [specific data types]. They cannot see [restricted data types]. Sports medicine has access to health-related data to make medical decisions.
Your Rights | You have the right to know what is collected, ask questions, and decline participation without penalty. If you consent, you can withdraw at any time.
Data After You Leave | When you graduate, your data is [retained for X years/deleted within X days]. If you transfer, [transfer protocol summary].
If Something Feels Wrong | If you feel stressed about your data, if someone is using it in a way that feels inappropriate, or if you have any questions, talk to [contact person/title]. You can also raise concerns through [SAAC/anonymous reporting process].
Develop a Coaches Education Module covering:
Overview of available performance technologies and what data they produce.
What data coaches are permitted to access and what is restricted (e.g., medical data, mental health screening results).
Limitations of performance technology data: these are tools, not crystal balls. Data should supplement coaching judgment, not replace it.
Responsible communication about data with student-athletes (avoid using data punitively or publicly).
The boundary between coaching decisions and medical decisions: sports medicine retains independent, unchallengeable authority over medical management and return-to-play.
Departmental policies and the consequences of policy violations.
Develop modules for S&C Staff, Sports Medicine, and Administration. Each should be tailored to their specific responsibilities as outlined in the audience focus table below:
Audience | Primary Focus Areas | Estimated Length
Student-Athletes | Rights, consent, data use, mental health, how to raise concerns | 20-30 min
Coaches | Responsible use, data access boundaries, limitations, independent medical authority | 30 min
S&C Staff | Device operation, data collection protocols, quality control, escalation to sports medicine | 30-45 min
Sports Medicine | Data-informed clinical decisions, independent medical authority, privacy obligations, return-to-play | 30 min
Administration | Policy compliance, risk management, legal obligations, procurement oversight, data security | 30 min
IT | Data storage, encryption, access controls, vendor security review, breach response protocols | 30 min
Strategy 2.3: Address Required Topics
NCAA Strategy:  Address topics  such as:  limitations and potential harms of performance technologies; data privacy and security; student-athlete rights and protections (e.g., informed consent); departmental policies and procedures for responsible use.
The NCAA names four specific topic areas. All four should appear in every audience module, though the depth and emphasis will vary. Below is a more detailed breakdown of what each topic should cover.
Required Topic | What to Cover | Why It Matters
1. Limitations & Potential Harms | No technology is perfectly accurate. Results can be misleading if context is missing. Mental health risks include data fixation, anxiety, body image concerns. Over-reliance on data can undermine coaching instincts and athlete autonomy. | Prevents overconfidence in data and protects student-athlete well-being.
2. Data Privacy & Security | What data is collected, where it is stored, who can access it, how long it is retained, what happens in a breach, and what laws apply (FERPA, state privacy, etc.). | Legal obligation and trust-building with student-athletes.
3. Student-Athlete Rights | Informed consent process, voluntary participation, right to withdraw, right to access own data, right to know how data is used, grievance process. | Foundational to ethical use and NCAA expectations.
4. Departmental Policies | Overview of the written plan, roles and responsibilities, technology evaluation process, feedback mechanisms, consequences for policy violations. | Ensures  everyone operates under the same standards.
Deliverable:
Five audience-specific training modules (slide decks and/or handouts) covering all four required topics, tailored to each group. Target completion: June 2026 for initial versions; reviewed and updated annually.
Recommendation 3: Data Management
What the NCAA Says: It is recommended that schools establish who owns data from performance technologies, where and how data is stored, who has the authority to access data and how data is permitted to be used. Performance technologies have different use-case scenarios and produce different types of data, and the interpretation and communication of data may benefit from a multidisciplinary approach.
What This Means for Baylor
This is the most complex recommendation because it sits at the intersection of legal, IT, sports medicine, and coaching. We need clear, documented answers to four questions: Who owns the data? Where does it live? Who can see it? What can it be used for? We also need specific protocols for transfer student-athletes and for situations where data informs medical decisions.
Strategy 3.1: Define Who Interprets and Shares Data
NCAA Strategy:  Determine who can be involved in interpreting and sharing/communicating data from performance technologies, including considerations for the required competencies and oversight necessary to do so effectively and responsibly.
Key Actions:
Create a Data Touchpoint Map. For every performance technology currently in use (identified during the technology inventory), document: what data it produces, who collects it, who interprets it, who it is shared with, and where it is stored.
Draft Template: Data Touchpoint Map
Technology | Data Produced | Collected By | Interpreted By | Shared With | Stored Where
[e.g., GPS Tracker] | Distance, speed, acceleration, player load | S&C Staff | S&C / Sport Scientist | Coaches (summary), Sports Med (if injury-related) | [Vendor cloud / campus server]
[e.g., Heart Rate Monitor] | HR, HRV, recovery metrics | S&C Staff | S&C / Sports Med | Sports Med (clinical), Coaches (aggregate only) | [Vendor platform]
[e.g., Body Comp Tool] | Body fat %, lean mass, etc. | Sports Med / S&C | Sports Med | Restricted: Sports Med only unless SA consents to share | [Campus server]
[e.g., Wellness Survey] | Sleep, soreness, stress, mood | S&C / Sports Med | Sports Med / Sport Psych | Coaches (flagged concerns only, no raw scores) | [Survey platform]
[Add rows as needed] |  |  |  |  | 
Define competency requirements for data interpretation. Not everyone should be interpreting every type of data. Establish minimum qualifications:
Health-related data (HRV, wellness, body composition): Interpretation restricted to sports medicine staff, licensed athletic trainers, or individuals with documented sports science credentials.
Training load and performance data (GPS, force plates, velocity): Interpretation by certified S&C professionals or individuals with sports science competencies.
Aggregate/summary data (team averages, trends): May be shared with coaches and administration in summarized form, with context provided by the interpreting professional.
Establish data sharing rules. Create a clear matrix showing who can share what with whom:
Data Type | Sports Med | S&C | Coaches | Administration | Student-Athlete
Individual health/medical | Full access | Flagged concerns only | No access | No access | Full access (own data)
Individual training load | Full access | Full access | Summary with context | No access | Full access (own data)
Individual body comp | Full access | With SA consent | No access | No access | Full access (own data)
Wellness survey (raw) | Full access | Flagged concerns only | No access | No access | Full access (own data)
Team aggregates | Full access | Full access | Full access | Summary reports | Team-level only
Assign a Data Steward. Designate one person responsible for overseeing compliance with data policies, managing access requests, and serving as the point of contact for data-related questions. Recommended: someone in sports medicine or athletics administration with IT coordination.
Deliverable:
Data Touchpoint Map and Data Access Matrix documents. Target: April 2026 (draft), May 2026 (finalized with legal review).
Strategy 3.2: Clarify Data Ownership and Rights
NCAA Strategy:  Determine what rights, if any, the school has with respect to data  collection, data use , data access and ownership of the performance technology data, including considerations for transfer student-athletes.
Key Actions:
Conduct a vendor contract audit. For every technology platform in use, pull the contract/terms of service and identify:
Who owns the data: Baylor, the student-athlete, or the vendor?
Where data is stored: On-premise, vendor cloud, third-party servers? In what jurisdiction?
Data retention: How long does the vendor keep data? Can we request deletion?
Data portability: Can we export our data if we switch vendors? In what format?
Breach notification: What is the vendor obligated to do if there is a data breach?
Work with legal to establish Baylor's position on data ownership. The recommendation is that Baylor assert ownership of all performance technology data collected from its student-athletes, with the student-athlete retaining the right to access their own data.
Develop a Transfer Student-Athlete Data Protocol:
Outgoing transfers: Student-athlete may request a copy of their data. Baylor retains its copy for [defined retention period]. Data is not proactively sent to the new school without the student-athlete's written request.
Incoming transfers: Baylor does not request performance technology data from the previous school. If the student-athlete voluntarily provides data, it is reviewed by sports medicine before being incorporated into Baylor systems.
Data deletion: Student-athletes may request deletion of their data upon departure, subject to any legal retention requirements.
Build data rights into the informed consent form. The consent form (see template below) should clearly state: what data is collected, how it will be used, who will access it, how long it will be retained, what happens at graduation/transfer, and how to withdraw consent.
Draft Template: Draft Informed Consent Form (Key Sections)
Section | Sample Language
Purpose | Baylor Athletics uses performance technologies to support your health, safety, and athletic performance. This form explains what data we collect, how we use it, and your rights regarding that data.
Technologies Used | [List specific technologies used by the student-athlete's sport, e.g., "Catapult GPS units during practice and competition, InBody body composition scans, daily wellness surveys via [platform]."]
Data Collected | The following types of data may be collected: [list specific data types, e.g., heart rate, GPS movement data, body composition measurements, sleep quality, self-reported wellness scores].
How Data Is Used | Your data will be used to: monitor training load and recovery, support injury prevention, inform return-to-play decisions (by sports medicine staff), and evaluate the effectiveness of training programs.
Who Has Access | Your data will be accessible to: [list specific roles and what they can see, consistent with the Data Access Matrix]. Your individual data will not be shared with anyone outside these roles without your written permission.
Your Rights | Participation is voluntary. You may decline to participate or withdraw consent at any time without penalty or impact on your athletic scholarship, playing time, or standing on the team. You have the right to: view your own data, ask questions about how it is used, and request corrections or deletion (subject to legal retention requirements).
Data Retention | Your data will be retained for [X years] after your departure from Baylor Athletics. After this period, data will be securely deleted. You may request earlier deletion upon departure.
Transfer Protocol | If you transfer to another institution, your data will not be sent to the new school without your written request. You may request a copy of your data at any time.
Contact | If you have questions or concerns about your data, contact [Data Steward name, title, email, phone].
Signature | I have read and understand this consent form. I voluntarily agree to participate in performance technology data collection as described above.  Student-Athlete Signature: _____________ Date: _______ Printed Name: _______________
Deliverable:
Informed Consent Form Template (reviewed and approved by legal). Transfer Student-Athlete Data Protocol (1-2 pages). Vendor Contract Audit Summary (spreadsheet). Target: May 2026.
Strategy 3.3: Establish Permissible Uses of Data
NCAA Strategy:  Clarify the school's permissible uses of data from performance technologies. If data might be used to inform medical decision-making, sports medicine staff should be involved. Schools should refer to independent medical care best practices to ensure the unchallengeable, autonomous authority of primary athletics healthcare providers to determine medical management and return-to-play decisions.
Key Actions:
Create an Approved Uses / Prohibited Uses list:
Approved Uses | Prohibited Uses
Monitoring training load to prevent overtraining | Using data to punish or publicly shame a student-athlete
Supporting injury prevention through workload management | Sharing individual data with media, NIL partners, or agents without written SA consent
Informing  return-to-play decisions (sports medicine only) | Using body composition data to restrict access to meals or dining
Evaluating effectiveness of training programs | Making  scholarship  or roster decisions based solely on technology data
Identifying trends that may indicate injury risk | Allowing coaches to override sports medicine return-to-play decisions based on performance data
Supporting sport science research (with IRB approval and SA consent) | Selling or sharing data with third parties
Providing student-athletes with their own data upon request | Retaining data beyond the stated retention period without legal basis
Codify independent medical authority. Include explicit language in the written plan stating that sports medicine staff retain final, unchallengeable authority over all medical management and return-to-play decisions, regardless of what performance technology data may suggest. Coaches and administrators may not override medical judgment based on data. Reference the NCAA Independent Medical Care Best Practices.
Coordinate with IT on data security. Work with IT to ensure:
All performance technology data is stored on encrypted systems.
Access is controlled through role-base

1	NCAA Performance Technologies
2	Recommendations
3	Comprehensive Action Plan for Baylor Athletics
4	Prepared by Coach Rash
5	Baylor University Department of Athletics
6	March 2026
7	WORKING DOCUMENT
8	For internal use. Subject to revision based on stakeholder input.
9	Table of Contents
10	Introduction
11	In March 2026, the NCAA Sport Science Institute published Performance Technologies Recommendations: Responsible Use in Collegiate Athletics, a consensus document developed from the May 2025 NCAA Summit on Performance Technologies. The document provides member schools with a framework for responsibly using performance technologies, organized around five core recommendations: Policy, Education, Data Management, Technology Selection, and Continuous Improvement.
12	This action plan translates those recommendations into a detailed, Baylor-specific implementation roadmap. Each section includes the NCAA language, what it means for our department, specific action items with assigned deliverables, and draft templates or sample language that the working group can adapt as we move forward.
13	Baylor Athletics does not currently have formal performance technology policies in place. This plan is designed to build the foundation from scratch, leveraging existing structures (annual compliance sessions, SAAC, campus IT, and legal resources) wherever possible.
14	How to Use This Document
15	Each recommendation section follows a consistent structure:
16	Blue callout box: The NCAA recommendation language, quoted directly.
17	Gold callout box: The specific NCAA strategy statement being addressed.
18	"What This Means for Baylor": Plain-language interpretation of how this applies to us.
19	Key Actions: Checkbox items for the working group to track.
20	Deliverable: The specific output expected from each action area.
21	Draft Templates: Sample language, forms, or frameworks ready for adaptation.
22	Recommendation 1: Policy
23	What the NCAA Says: It is recommended that schools establish a written plan that addresses the responsible use of performance technologies. Having a written plan can help establish common standards and procedures, increase transparency ,  and address school-specific needs and resources.
24	What This Means for Baylor
25	We need a formal, written policy document that serves as the governing framework for how Baylor Athletics uses performance technologies. This is not a one-time exercise. The NCAA expects it to be developed by a cross-functional team, reviewed regularly, and updated as technologies and needs evolve. Every other recommendation in this document (education, data management, purchasing, and feedback) ties back to this written plan.
26	Strategy 1.1: Assemble a Multidisciplinary Working Group
27	NCAA Strategy:  Engage a multidisciplinary team in developing, routinely reviewing ,  and revising a written plan, leveraging existing campus resources and systems. Key roles on that team may include, but are not limited to, student-athletes, sports medicine staff, coaches, athletics administration, legal affairs ,  and information technology.
28	Key Actions:
29	Identify a chair/lead for the working group. This person should have the organizational authority to coordinate across departments and the bandwidth to drive the process forward. Recommended candidates: Associate AD for Student-Athlete Services, Director of Sports Medicine, or a senior administrator with cross-departmental oversight.
30	Recruit representatives from each required area. The NCAA specifically names the following roles. Each representative should have decision-making authority or direct access to decision-makers in their area:
31	Student-Athletes: Minimum two representatives, ideally from different sports and genders. SAAC members or sport captains are strong candidates. Their voice is not advisory; it is essential.
32	Sports Medicine/Athletic Training: Head athletic trainer or designee. This person will be critical for data management (Rec 3) and ensuring the independent medical authority is protected.
33	Strength and Conditioning: Director of S&C or senior staff member. S&C is typically the primary operator of wearable technologies and force plates.
34	Coaching: Minimum two sport representatives from different sports. Coaches are end-users of performance data and need a seat at the table.
35	Athletics Administration: Associate AD or senior administrator who can approve policy and allocate resources.
36	Legal Affairs/Compliance: University legal counsel or athletics compliance officer. Essential for data privacy, consent, and regulatory considerations.
37	Information Technology: Campus IT or athletics IT representative. Responsible for data security, storage, vendor integration, and breach response.
38	Define the group charter. The working group should have a clear written charter that includes:
39	Mission: Develop, maintain, and oversee Baylor Athletics' written plan for the responsible use of performance technologies.
40	Scope: All performance technologies used across Baylor Athletics, including devices, software, apps, and surveys that collect biometric or performance data.
41	Responsibilities: Draft and maintain the written plan, review and approve new technology purchases, oversee education programs, collect and act on feedback, and ensure compliance with applicable laws.
42	Meeting cadence: Monthly during initial development (March through June 2026), then quarterly once the plan is established.
43	Decision-making: Consensus-based where possible; chair breaks ties. Legal has veto authority on compliance matters.
44	Set the initial meeting schedule. Book monthly meetings through June 2026. The first meeting should focus on reviewing this document and the NCAA source material, and on assigning ownership of plan sections.
45	Deliverable:
46	Working Group Charter Document (1-2 pages) documenting mission, membership, roles, meeting cadence, and decision-making process.
47	Draft Template: Working Group Charter
48	Section | Content
49	Purpose | Establish and maintain Baylor Athletics' written plan for the responsible use of performance technologies in alignment with NCAA Sport Science Institute recommendations.
50	Membership | Chair: [TBD] Student-Athletes: [Names, Sports] Sports Medicine: [Name, Title] S&C: [Name, Title] Coaching: [Name, Sport] and [Name, Sport] Administration: [Name, Title] Legal/Compliance: [Name, Title] IT: [Name, Title]
51	Meeting Cadence | Monthly (March-June 2026), Quarterly (July 2026 onward)
52	Responsibilities | 1. Develop written plan 2. Review/approve new technology purchases 3. Oversee education programs 4. Collect and act on feedback 5. Ensure legal/regulatory compliance
53	Decision Process | Consensus-based; Chair breaks ties. Legal holds veto on compliance matters.
54	Reporting | Chair reports to [AD/Senior Administrator] after each meeting.
55	Review | Charter reviewed annually at the first meeting of each academic year.
56	Strategy 1.2: Draft the Written Plan
57	NCAA Strategy:  Address school-specific considerations, including how relevant groups will be educated, how data will be managed, how decisions will be made about selecting and implementing new technologies and how continuous improvement will be approached.
58	The written plan is the central deliverable. It should be a single, comprehensive document (or a policy manual with clearly organized sections) that anyone in the department can reference. Below is the recommended structure and the content each section should address.
59	Key Actions:
60	Create a policy document organized around the following sections:
61	Plan Section | Content to Address | Owner
62	1. Purpose & Scope | Why the plan exists, what it covers, which technologies and personnel fall under it | Chair
63	2. Definitions | Performance technology, biometric data, performance data, informed consent, data steward, etc. | Chair + Legal
64	3. Roles & Responsibilities | Who does what : Working Group, coaches, S&C, sports medicine, IT, student-athletes, administration | Chair
65	4. Student-Athlete Rights | Informed consent process, right to decline, data access rights, grievance process | Legal
66	5. Data Governance | Data ownership, storage, access controls, retention, transfer protocol, breach response (see Rec 3) | IT + Legal
67	6. Technology Evaluation | Criteria and process for vetting new technologies before purchase (see Rec 4) | S&C + Sports Med
68	7. Education Requirements | Who gets trained, how often, on what topics, and how completion is tracked (see Rec 2) | Chair
69	8. Continuous Improvement | Feedback mechanisms, annual review process, plan revision protocol (see Rec 5) | Chair
70	9. Compliance | Applicable laws (FERPA, state privacy, biometric), NCAA guidance references, institutional policies | Legal + Compliance
71	10. Appendices | Consent form template, tech evaluation checklist, education curriculum outlines, feedback survey | Various
72	Route the draft through legal affairs and compliance for review. Legal should review for: applicable privacy laws (FERPA, Texas data privacy, any biometric privacy considerations), adequacy of informed consent language, data breach notification obligations, and alignment with university-wide policies.
73	Establish version control. Use a naming convention (e.g., BaylorAthletics_PerfTech_Policy_v1.0_2026-06) and maintain a revision log on the first page of the document. Store the master copy in a central location accessible to all working group members.
74	Set an annual review date. The plan should be reviewed at least annually. Recommend tying the review to the start of each academic year (August/September) so updates can be communicated during preseason meetings.
75	Deliverable:
76	Baylor Athletics Performance Technology Policy (estimated 15-25 pages with appendices). Target completion: June 2026.
77	Milestone | Description | Target Date
78	Working Group Formed | Chair identified, members recruited, charter signed | March 2026
79	First Meeting | Review  the  NCAA document, assign plan sections to owners | Early April 2026
80	Section Drafts Due | Each owner submits their section draft to the chair | Late April 2026
81	Full Draft Assembled | Chair compiles all sections into  a  unified document | Early May 2026
82	Legal/Compliance Review | Legal reviews full draft, provides redlines | Mid-May 2026
83	Working Group Final Review | Group reviews legal feedback, makes final edits | Late May 2026
84	Plan Approved | Chair and AD sign off; plan distributed to department | June 2026
85	First Annual Review | Working group reviews and updates the plan | August/September 2026
86	Recommendation 2: Education
87	What the NCAA Says: It is recommended that schools routinely provide education about the responsible use of performance technologies to those involved with their use. Education is foundational for informed consent, and it aids in ensuring schools use performance technologies in a way that maximizes benefits and minimizes harm to student-athletes.
88	What This Means for Baylor
89	Everyone who touches performance technology needs training, and that training needs to happen at least once a year. The good news: Baylor already has annual compliance and onboarding sessions. We can build performance technology modules into those existing structures rather than creating an entirely new training apparatus. The key is tailoring the content to different audiences, because a student-athlete and a compliance officer need very different information.
90	Strategy 2.1: Provide Annual Education to All Involved
91	NCAA Strategy:  At least once annually, provide education to those involved in selecting, using or accessing data from performance technologies.
92	Key Actions:
93	Map every person/role that interacts with performance technology. Create a comprehensive list of who selects, operates, interprets, accesses, or makes decisions based on performance technology data. This becomes your required-training roster.
94	Integrate performance technology training into existing annual sessions:
95	Staff annual compliance meeting: Add a 30-45 minute performance technology module covering policy overview, data handling responsibilities, and any updates from the previous year.
96	New student-athlete orientation: Add a 20-30 minute segment on performance technology rights, informed consent, what data is collected, and how to raise concerns.
97	Returning student-athlete preseason meeting: Add a brief (10-15 minute) refresher covering any new technologies introduced, policy changes, or updated consent requirements.
98	New hire onboarding: Include performance technology policy review for any new coaches, S&C staff, athletic trainers, or administrators.
99	Create an attendance tracking system. Use sign-in sheets or digital tracking (LMS if available) to document who completed training and when. This is your compliance record if questions arise.
100	Store all training materials centrally. Maintain a shared folder (e.g., on the athletics shared drive or LMS) with all slide decks, handouts, and reference materials so staff can review them at any time.
101	Deliverable:
102	An annual education calendar that maps each audience to their training session, timing, and delivery method.
103	Draft Template: Annual Education Calendar
104	Audience | Session | Timing | Duration | Delivery | Tracked?
105	All Staff | Annual Compliance Meeting | August (preseason) | 30-45 min | In-person | Sign-in sheet
106	New Student-Athletes | Orientation | August/January | 20-30 min | In-person | Sign-in sheet
107	Returning SAs | Preseason Meeting | August | 10-15 min | In-person | Sign-in sheet
108	New Hires | Onboarding | Within 30 days of hire | 30 min | 1-on-1 or small group | HR checklist
109	Working Group | Annual Review Meeting | September | 60-90 min | In-person | Meeting minutes
110	Strategy 2.2: Tailor Education by Audience
111	NCAA Strategy:  Educational needs are likely to vary among different groups and schools should consider tailoring education to meet each group's learning needs. Such groups may include, but are not limited to, student-athletes, coaches, strength and conditioning staff, sports medicine staff and administration.
112	A one-size-fits-all presentation will not work. Below is a detailed breakdown of what each audience needs to know, along with sample talking points and curriculum outlines.
113	Key Actions:
114	Develop a Student-Athlete Education Module covering:
115	What performance technologies are and why Baylor uses them.
116	Exactly what data is collected about them (types, frequency, devices).
117	Who can see their data and who cannot (access controls by role).
118	How their data is stored, how long it is kept, and what happens when they graduate or transfer.
119	Their right to informed consent: what they are agreeing to, that participation is voluntary, how to withdraw, and that declining will not affect their standing on the team.
120	Potential negative effects to watch for (data fixation, anxiety about metrics, body image concerns from body composition tracking) and who to talk to if they experience them.
121	How to raise concerns or file a complaint about how their data is being used.
122	Draft Template: Sample Student-Athlete Talking Points
123	Topic | Key Message
124	What We Collect | We use [GPS trackers/heart rate monitors/body comp tools/wellness surveys/etc.] to help us keep you healthy and help you perform your best. Here is specifically what each tool measures.
125	Who Sees It | Your data is shared only with [specific roles]. Coaches can see [specific data types]. They cannot see [restricted data types]. Sports medicine has access to health-related data to make medical decisions.
126	Your Rights | You have the right to know what is collected, ask questions, and decline participation without penalty. If you consent, you can withdraw at any time.
127	Data After You Leave | When you graduate, your data is [retained for X years/deleted within X days]. If you transfer, [transfer protocol summary].
128	If Something Feels Wrong | If you feel stressed about your data, if someone is using it in a way that feels inappropriate, or if you have any questions, talk to [contact person/title]. You can also raise concerns through [SAAC/anonymous reporting process].
129	Develop a Coaches Education Module covering:
130	Overview of available performance technologies and what data they produce.
131	What data coaches are permitted to access and what is restricted (e.g., medical data, mental health screening results).
132	Limitations of performance technology data: these are tools, not crystal balls. Data should supplement coaching judgment, not replace it.
133	Responsible communication about data with student-athletes (avoid using data punitively or publicly).
134	The boundary between coaching decisions and medical decisions: sports medicine retains independent, unchallengeable authority over medical management and return-to-play.
135	Departmental policies and the consequences of policy violations.

137	Audience | Primary Focus Areas | Estimated Length
138	Student-Athletes | Rights, consent, data use, mental health, how to raise concerns | 20-30 min
139	Coaches | Responsible use, data access boundaries, limitations, independent medical authority | 30 min
140	S&C Staff | Device operation, data collection protocols, quality control, escalation to sports medicine | 30-45 min
141	Sports Medicine | Data-informed clinical decisions, independent medical authority, privacy obligations, return-to-play | 30 min
142	Administration | Policy compliance, risk management, legal obligations, procurement oversight, data security | 30 min
143	IT | Data storage, encryption, access controls, vendor security review, breach response protocols | 30 min

145	NCAA Strategy:  Address topics  such as:  limitations and potential harms of performance technologies; data privacy and security; student-athlete rights and protections (e.g., informed consent); departmental policies and procedures for responsible use.

Over-reliance on data can undermine coaching instincts and athlete autonomy. | Prevents overconfidence in data and protects student-athlete well-being.
149	2. Data Privacy & Security | What data is collected, where it is stored, who can access it, how long it is retained, what happens in a breach, and what laws apply (FERPA, state privacy, etc.). | Legal obligation and trust-building with student-athletes.
150	3. Student-Athlete Rights | Informed consent process, voluntary participation, right to withdraw, right to access own data, right to know how data is used, grievance process. | Foundational to ethical use and NCAA expectations.
151	4. Departmental Policies | Overview of the written plan, roles and responsibilities, technology evaluation process, feedback mechanisms, consequences for policy violations. | Ensures  everyone operates under the same standards.
152	Deliverable:
153	Five audience-specific training modules (slide decks and/or handouts) covering all four required topics, tailored to each group. Target completion: June 2026 for initial versions; reviewed and updated annually.

185	Key Actions:

205	Your Rights | Participation is voluntary. You may decline to participate or withdraw consent at any time without penalty or impact on your athletic scholarship, playing time, or standing on the team. You have the right to: view your own data, ask questions about how it is used, and request corrections or deletion (subject to legal retention requirements).
206	Data Retention | Your data will be retained for [X years] after your departure from Baylor Athletics. After this period, data will be securely deleted. You may request earlier deletion upon departure.
207	Transfer Protocol | If you transfer to another institution, your data will not be sent to the new school without your written request. You may request a copy of your data at any time.
208	Contact | If you have questions or concerns about your data, contact [Data Steward name, title, email, phone].
209	Signature | I have read and understand this consent form. I voluntarily agree to participate in performance technology data collection as described above.  Student-Athlete Signature: _____________ Date: _______ Printed Name: _______________
210	Deliverable:
211	Informed Consent Form Template (reviewed and approved by legal). Transfer Student-Athlete Data Protocol (1-2 pages). Vendor Contract Audit Summary (spreadsheet). Target: May 2026.
212	Strategy 3.3: Establish Permissible Uses of Data
213	NCAA Strategy:  Clarify the school's permissible uses of data from performance technologies. If data might be used to inform medical decision-making, sports medicine staff should be involved. Schools should refer to independent medical care best practices to ensure the unchallengeable, autonomous authority of primary athletics healthcare providers to determine medical management and return-to-play decisions.
214	Key Actions:
215	Create an Approved Uses / Prohibited Uses list:
216	Approved Uses | Prohibited Uses
217	Monitoring training load to prevent overtraining | Using data to punish or publicly shame a student-athlete
218	Supporting injury prevention through workload management | Sharing individual data with media, NIL partners, or agents without written SA consent
219	Informing  return-to-play decisions (sports medicine only) | Using body composition data to restrict access to meals or dining
220	Evaluating effectiveness of training programs | Making  scholarship  or roster decisions based solely on technology data
221	Identifying trends that may indicate injury risk | Allowing coaches to override sports medicine return-to-play decisions based on performance data
222	Supporting sport science research (with IRB approval and SA consent) | Selling or sharing data with third parties
223	Providing student-athletes with their own data upon request | Retaining data beyond the stated retention period without legal basis
224	Codify independent medical authority. Include explicit language in the written plan stating that sports medicine staff retain final, unchallengeable authority over all medical management and return-to-play decisions, regardless of what performance technology data may suggest. Coaches and administrators may not override medical judgment based on data. Reference the NCAA Independent Medical Care Best Practices.
225	Coordinate with IT on data security. Work with IT to ensure:
226	All performance technology data is stored on encrypted systems.
227	Access is controlled through role-based permissions (matching the Data Access Matrix).
228	Backup and disaster recovery procedures are in place.
229	A data breach response plan exists and is tested.
230	Deliverable:
231	Approved/Prohibited Uses Policy (included in the written plan). Independent Medical Authority Statement (included in the written plan). IT Data Security Checklist (coordinated with campus IT). Target: May 2026.
232	Recommendation 4: Selecting & Implementing New Technologies
233	What the NCAA Says: It is recommended that schools establish a structured process for making decisions about selecting and implementing new performance technologies. A structured process that considers how to use performance technologies in a way that maximizes benefits and minimizes harm is important to ensure student-athlete well-being is prioritized.
234	What This Means for Baylor
235	No more ad hoc purchasing. Every new technology, whether it is a wearable device, a software platform, a mobile app, or a survey tool, should go through a defined evaluation process before it is purchased and deployed. The NCAA wants this to be a group decision driven by evidence, not a single department acting on vendor marketing.
236	Strategy 4.1: Use Evidence-Based Evaluation Standards
237	NCAA Strategy:  Review technologies using existing, evidence-based standards and frameworks that evaluate their value, usability ,  and quality.
238	Key Actions:
239	Develop a Technology Evaluation Checklist that every proposed technology must complete before purchase approval. The checklist should be filled out by the requesting department and reviewed by the Working Group.
240	Draft Template: Technology Evaluation Checklist
241	Evaluation Criteria | Questions to Answer | Score (1-5)
242	1. Scientific Validity | Is there peer-reviewed research supporting the technology's claims? Has it been validated in collegiate or athletic populations? Are the vendor's claims backed by independent evidence? | [  ]
243	2. Accuracy | Does the device measure what it claims to measure? What is the margin of error? Has accuracy been tested across different conditions (e.g., different sports, environments)? | [  ]
244	3. Reliability | Does the device produce consistent results under the same conditions? What is the test-retest reliability? | [  ]
245	4. Data Security | Where is data stored? Is it encrypted? Who has access? What is the vendor's breach notification policy? Is the vendor compliant with relevant regulations? | [  ]
246	5. Data Portability | Can data be exported in standard formats? What happens to data if we discontinue the platform? | [  ]
247	6. Usability | How easy is it to use for staff and student-athletes? What training is required? Is the user interface intuitive? | [  ]
248	7. Integration | Does it integrate with our existing systems? Are there compatibility issues with other technologies we use? | [  ]
249	8. Cost-Benefit | What is the total cost (purchase, subscription, maintenance, training)? Does the expected value justify the expense? What is the expected ROI? | [  ]
250	9. Fit with Program Needs | Does this technology solve an actual problem we have? Or is it a solution looking for a problem? Is there a cheaper or simpler alternative? | [  ]
251	10. Student-Athlete Impact | Could this technology have unintended negative effects on student-athlete well-being? Does it require significant time or effort from student-athletes? | [  ]
252	Scoring: 1 = Does not meet criteria, 5 = Fully meets criteria. A technology should score at a minimum of 3 on every criterion and achieve an average of 3.5 or above to proceed. Any score of 1 on Data Security or Student-Athlete Impact is an automatic rejection.
253	Deliverable:
254	Technology Evaluation Checklist Template (1-page form + scoring rubric). Target: May 2026.
255	Strategy 4.2: Assess Quality Before Committing
256	NCAA Strategy:  Consider and assess the quality of performance technologies. Quality may include, but is not limited to, factors such as accuracy, reliability, validity ,  and function.
257	Key Actions:
258	Require a pilot/trial period before full purchase whenever possible. Negotiate with vendors for a 30–60-day trial with a single sport or team before committing to a department-wide purchase. During the pilot, collect structured user feedback.
259	Request validation data from vendors. Ask for independent (non-vendor-funded) research demonstrating accuracy and reliability. If no independent research exists, that is a red flag worth noting on the evaluation checklist.
260	Check with peer institutions. Before purchasing, reach out to at least two comparable programs (Big 12 or Power conference) to ask about their experience with the technology. Document the feedback.
261	Conduct a post-implementation review. 90 days after deploying a new technology, the requesting department should report back to the Working Group on: whether the technology is performing as expected, user satisfaction, any issues encountered, and whether it should continue.
262	Draft Template: Pilot Evaluation Report
263	Section | Content
264	Technology Name | [Name, vendor, version]
265	Pilot Duration | [Start date] to [End date]
266	Sport/Team | [Sport used during pilot]
267	Requesting Department | [S&C / Sports Med / Coaching / etc.]
268	Purpose | Why we are evaluating this technology and what problem it is intended to solve.
269	Evaluation Checklist Score | [Overall score from the Technology Evaluation Checklist]
270	Pilot Findings | Did the technology perform as claimed? Were there accuracy or reliability issues? How did staff and student-athletes respond?
271	User Feedback Summary | What did staff say? What did student-athletes say?
272	Issues Encountered | Any technical problems, data security concerns, integration challenges, or negative student-athlete feedback?
273	Recommendation | Approve for full purchase / Extend pilot / Do not purchase. Rationale:
274	Submitted By | [Name, Title, Date]
275	Strategy 4.3: Multidisciplinary Purchase Decisions
276	NCAA Strategy:  Decisions about selecting and implementing performance technologies should be made by a multidisciplinary group. Important roles to consider  include sports medicine staff and individuals with competencies in sports science, coaching staff, information technology, data security, administration,  and compliance.
277	Key Actions:
278	Route all new technology purchase requests through the Working Group. No performance technology should be purchased without Working Group review and approval. This includes free tools, trial conversions, and platforms offered through sponsorship deals.
279	Establish a standard purchase request process:
280	Step 1: Requesting department completes the Technology Evaluation Checklist.
281	Step 2: IT reviews the data security section and provides written clearance or flags concerns.
282	Step 3: Sports medicine reviews student-athlete health/safety implications.
283	Step 4: Legal/compliance reviews vendor contract terms, data ownership, and regulatory considerations.
284	Step 5: Working Group reviews full package and votes to approve, request a pilot, or deny.
285	Step 6: If approved, finance/administration handles procurement. If a pilot is requested, see the pilot process above.
286	Document every decision. Maintain a log of all technology requests, evaluation scores, decisions, and rationale. This creates an audit trail and supports future decision-making.
287	Deliverable:
288	Technology Purchase Request Process (flowchart + written procedure). Purchase Decision Log (spreadsheet). Target: May 2026.
289	Recommendation 5: Continuous Improvement
290	What the NCAA Says: It is recommended that schools routinely get feedback from those using performance technologies about how these technologies are being used and how they are working. This feedback can be used to inform  changes  to the school's written plan to reflect current needs, available resources and evolving technological developments.
291	What This Means for Baylor
292	The written plan is a living document. The NCAA expects us to actively monitor how technologies are being used, whether they are delivering value, and, most importantly, whether student-athletes are experiencing any negative effects. Student-athlete feedback is not a nice-to-have; the NCAA calls it "critical." We need structured mechanisms to collect, interpret, and act on feedback from all stakeholders.
293	Strategy 5.1: Multidisciplinary Feedback Collection
294	NCAA Strategy:  Engage a multidisciplinary group to plan, collect ,  and interpret feedback about performance technologies. When possible, this group should include individuals involved in establishing the school's written plan for responsible use.
295	Key Actions:
296	Task the Working Group with leading the annual feedback cycle. The same group that developed the plan should be evaluating its effectiveness. This ensures continuity and accountability.
297	Schedule an Annual Performance Technology Review Meeting (separate from regular Working Group meetings). This dedicated session should:
298	Review all feedback collected during the year (surveys, focus groups, incident reports).
299	Evaluate each technology against its stated purpose: is it delivering the expected value?
300	Identify any policy gaps, compliance issues, or areas where the plan needs updating.
301	Set priorities for the coming year (new trainings needed, technologies to add or remove, policy revisions).
302	Document decisions and updates in the plan revision log.
303	Produce an Annual Performance Technology Report (2-3 pages) summarizing findings and actions taken. Share with athletics administration.
304	Deliverable:
305	Annual Performance Technology Review Meeting Agenda Template and Annual Report Template. Target: First cycle completes Spring 2027.
306	Draft Template: Annual Review Meeting Agenda
307	Agenda Item | Led By | Time
308	1. Review of feedback: student-athlete survey results | Chair / Student-Athlete Reps | 20 min
309	2. Review of feedback: staff survey  results/observations | Chair | 15 min
310	3. Technology-by-technology effectiveness review | S&C / Sports Med | 20 min
311	4. Education program assessment:  Did  training meet needs? | Chair | 10 min
312	5. Policy compliance review: any incidents or gaps? | Legal / Compliance | 10 min
313	6. Proposed plan updates for  the  coming year | All | 15 min
314	7. Action items and next steps | Chair | 10 min
315	Strategy 5.2: Prioritize Student-Athlete Feedback
316	NCAA Strategy:  Understanding student-athletes' experiences with performance technology is critical. Schools should obtain student-athlete feedback to learn about the positive and/or negative impacts performance technology use has on their student-athletes.
317	Student-athlete feedback is the most important input in the continuous improvement process. The NCAA uses the word "critical" deliberately. We need a structured way to hear from student-athletes that goes beyond assuming they are fine because they have not complained.
318	Key Actions:
319	Develop an annual student-athlete survey. Administer once per year (recommended: end of spring semester) to capture the full year’s experience. Keep it short (10-15 questions) to maximize response rates.
320	Draft Template: Draft Student-Athlete Performance Technology Survey
321	# | Question | Response Type
322	1 | I understand what performance technology data is collected about me. | Strongly Disagree to Strongly Agree (1-5)
323	2 | I understand who has access to my data and how it is used. | 1-5 scale
324	3 | I feel comfortable with how my data is being used. | 1-5 scale
325	4 | I was given adequate information before consenting to data collection. | 1-5 scale
326	5 | I feel that I can decline participation without negative consequences. | 1-5 scale
327	6 | The performance technologies used in my sport have helped my training or performance. | 1-5 scale
328	7 | I have experienced stress, anxiety, or negative feelings related to performance technology data (e.g., fixation on scores, body image concerns). | Never / Rarely / Sometimes / Often / Always
329	8 | If I had a concern about how my data was being used, I would know who to contact. | Yes / No / Unsure
330	9 | I have raised a concern about performance technology this year. | Yes / No
331	10 | If yes, my concern was addressed satisfactorily. | Yes / No / N/A
332	11 | The training I received about performance technology was helpful. | 1-5 scale
333	12 | Is there anything about how Baylor uses performance technology that you think could be improved? | Open text
334	13 | Is there anything about your experience with performance technology that concerns you? | Open text
335	Supplement surveys with qualitative feedback. Consider one or two annual focus group sessions with student-athletes from different sports. SAAC meetings can also serve as a forum for surfacing concerns. Qualitative feedback captures nuance that Likert scales miss.
336	Establish a confidential concern reporting channel. Student-athletes should have a way to raise concerns outside of surveys. This could be a dedicated email address, an anonymous online form, or a designated point of contact (e.g., the Data Steward or a member of the Student-Athlete Advisory Committee).
337	Share results with student-athletes. Close the feedback loop. Share a brief summary of survey findings and any actions taken at a SAAC meeting or through team communication. This builds trust and encourages future participation.
338	Deliverable:
339	Annual Student-Athlete Survey (digital, administered via survey platform). Confidential Concern Reporting Channel (email or anonymous form). Target: Survey launches Spring 2027; reporting channel established Fall 2026.
340	Strategy 5.3: Evaluate Implementation and Effectiveness
341	NCAA Strategy:  Areas for feedback from additional groups could  include:  technology implementation (e.g., how  were technologies  used),  technology  effectiveness (e.g., how did outcomes align with the school's reasons for their use), and education (e.g., does education meet  learner  needs).
342	Key Actions:
343	Develop a Staff Feedback Survey (brief, annual). Administer to all staff involved with performance technologies.
344	Draft Template: Draft Staff Performance Technology Survey
345	# | Question | Response Type
346	1 | The technologies I use are reliable and perform as expected. | 1-5 scale
347	2 | I have adequate training  to use  the technologies assigned to me. | 1-5 scale
348	3 | The data I receive from performance technologies is useful for my work. | 1-5 scale
349	4 | I understand the department's policies on performance technology use. | 1-5 scale
350	5 | I know who to contact if I have a data-related question or concern. | Yes / No
351	6 | Are there technologies you think we should add, change, or discontinue? Why? | Open text
352	7 | Is there additional training you would find helpful? | Open text
353	Conduct a technology-by-technology effectiveness review. For each technology in use, the Working Group should evaluate annually:
354	Implementation: Are we using it the way we intended? Are all staff following protocols?
355	Effectiveness: Are the outcomes matching the reasons we adopted it? Is it delivering measurable value?
356	Student-athlete impact: Is it causing any reported negative effects?
357	Cost: Is the ongoing cost justified by the value delivered?
358	Decision: Continue as-is / Modify usage / Discontinue.
359	Evaluate education effectiveness. Use training attendance records, survey feedback (both SA and staff), and observed knowledge gaps to determine whether education programs are landing. Update curriculum as needed.
360	Deliverable:
361	Annual Staff Survey, Technology Effectiveness Review Template, and Education Effectiveness Assessment. All part of the annual review cycle beginning Spring 2027.
362	Master Implementation Timeline
363	The following consolidates all five recommendations into a single timeline. The approach builds the foundation quickly, leverages existing structures, and targets full implementation by the start of the 2026-27 academic year, with the first complete feedback cycle closing in Spring 2027.
364	When | Key Deliverables | Rec. #
365	Mar 2026 | Form  Working Group, approve charter, conduct technology inventory, schedule legal meeting | 1, 3
366	Apr 2026 | Present  the  NCAA doc to S-A Staff, begin drafting written plan sections, start vendor contract audit | 1, 2, 3
367	May 2026 | Complete legal review of plan and consent form, finalize Data Access Matrix, build Tech Evaluation Checklist | 1, 3, 4
368	Jun 2026 | Finalize and approve  the  written plan, develop all education modules,  and  establish  a  confidential reporting channel | 1, 2
369	Jul 2026 | Distribute  plan  to all staff, begin updating consent forms for incoming student-athletes | 1, 2, 3
370	Aug 2026 | Deliver staff training at annual compliance meeting, SA training at orientation,  and  roll out updated consent process | 2, 3
371	Sep 2026 | Returning SA refresher during preseason, Working Group quarterly meeting, activate Tech Purchase Process | 2, 4
372	Fall 2026 | Full operation under new policies, collect informal feedback, document any incidents or issues | All
373	Jan 2027 | Mid-year Working Group check-in, address any urgent issues, new SA onboarding for spring admits | 1, 2
374	Spring 2027 | Administer SA and staff surveys, conduct technology effectiveness review, hold Annual Review Meeting, update plan | 5
375	Summary of Key Deliverables
376	Deliverable | Owner | Target Date
377	Working Group Charter | Chair (TBD) | March 2026
378	Technology Inventory | S&C + Sports Med | March 2026
379	Data Touchpoint Map | Working Group | April 2026
380	Data Access Matrix | Working Group + Legal | May 2026
381	Vendor Contract Audit | Legal + IT | May 2026
382	Informed Consent Form Template | Legal | May 2026
383	Technology Evaluation Checklist | S&C + Sports Med | May 2026
384	Transfer SA Data Protocol | Legal + Sports Med | May 2026
385	Written Policy (full plan) | Working Group | June 2026
386	Education Modules (5 audiences) | Chair + Subject Leads | June 2026
387	Confidential Reporting Channel | Administration | June 2026
388	Annual SA Survey | Chair + Student-Athlete Reps | Spring 2027
389	Annual Staff Survey | Chair | Spring 2027
390	Annual Performance Tech Report | Chair | Spring 2027
391	Closing
392	This plan is designed to be thorough but practical. We are leveraging existing structures wherever we can (annual compliance sessions, SAAC, campus IT, and legal), so this does not become an unsustainable burden on top of everything else the department is managing. The Working Group is the engine that keeps all of this moving, which is why standing it up first is the immediate priority.
393	This is a working document. It will get better with input from the people in the room. I am ready to start pulling the group together as soon as you give the green light.
